doc.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014

title: Jazz as life, not politics: message and pioneering racial integration
summary: Harper says players like Roach saw jazz as saying something about humanity and that jazz musicians pioneered racial mixing.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: His music took a political stance often, and there was something on your website I saw where you said, if everyone listened to jazz once a day that it could make a difference in the world. And I wonder if you still feel that way.

Sure. Because I think, I guess Max’s stance could be viewed as political. I view it more as life. And that’s what I meant. I think that music to them was much more important than it is for a lot of people today. And I mean some of the musicians playing it. Because their playing it wasn’t just to be playing to make music or just to make money or just ‘cause I can do it. They were still trying to say something through the music. And when you go back and you listen and read some interviews you’ll hear them talk about that, through the music. They were saying something. Because they came through a time which is not much different from everything that’s going on in the news today. It’s not much different than what we’re dealing with today. And they were dealing with it then and they were trying to say through the music, look we are all human. This is life. And to me nothing says that as much as jazz does.

Because I think it’s always been — it’s pioneered a lot of things. It’s gone into a lot of places, a lot of countries, and brought people together. It’s made people respect, I think too, in terms of dealing with some of the racial issues I think the jazz musicians and the music, without a lot of people talking about this, went to the forefront of a lot of that, pioneering, and that has to be talked about. Even a lot of other things we’ve seen the jazz musicians were some of the first people to go into these places or do some of these things, and because of them playing the music people had to say wait a minute, this is not easy stuff that these guys were doing. So that already debunked the myth that these people are unintelligent. So for the guys to get the sound and play the things they were playing and for them being investigated, and then for them to be gracious and giving

enough to say, come on, I can show you. And they were some of the first ones. You know you would go into some of those after-hours places and you’ll see all kinds of people, white, black people, just enjoying the music. And you’d start seeing guys play together. And on the bandstand, look, I’m going to hire this person because I like what they can do, they should be heard. You know what I mean? So the music, to me, through my studying would be inside the forefront of a lot of it. And I think it still should be.
